titulo: What Really Happens When You Tap Your Credit Card
descripcion: What happens in the two seconds after you tap: what your card number encodes, how the chip makes a one-time cryptogram, why phone payments use tokens, the journey through acquirer, network and issuer, who pays the hidden interchange fee, and the math of minimum payments. Educational content, not financial advice.

escenas.texto: You tap your card. Two seconds later, it beeps. In those two seconds, your payment crossed at least four companies, passed a cryptographic test, and got scored by an AI for fraud.
Visa says its network can handle up to eighty three thousand of these messages every second. Let's follow one, from the plastic in your hand to the money leaving your account.
Chapter one. The number.

visual.sub: sixteen digits with a secret structure

escenas.texto: Your card number isn't random. The first digit tells you the network. A four is Visa. A five is usually Mastercard.
The first six or eight digits identify the bank that issued it. The industry moved to eight digit bank numbers in twenty twenty two, because it was running out.
The middle digits are your account. And the very last digit is a check digit, calculated from all the others with a formula from the nineteen fifties called the Luhn algorithm.
Here's how it works. Starting from the right, double every second digit. If a result is more than nine, subtract nine. Add everything up. For a valid card, the total ends in zero.

items.texto: From the right, double every 2nd digit

escenas.texto: It's not security. It's a typo detector. Swap two neighboring digits or mistype one, and the website knows instantly, before anything is even sent to the bank.
Chapter two. The chip.
The magnetic stripe on the back is ancient technology. It stores the same data every time, so anyone who reads it once can copy it. That's how skimmers work.

The chip is different. It's a tiny computer with a secret key that never leaves the silicon. For every purchase, it mixes that key with the amount, the date and a counter, and produces a unique code called a cryptogram.

visual.nota: secret key + amount + date + counter → cryptogram

escenas.texto: Your bank recalculates that code. If it matches, the card is real. And because the counter goes up with every purchase, a copied code is useless the next time.

visual.etiqueta: a stolen code is worthless next time

escenas.texto: Chapter three. Tap and phone.
Tapping uses the same chip, just over radio. It's called near field communication, and it only works across a few centimeters, which is why you have to almost touch the reader.

visual.nota: NFC: works only within a few centimeters

escenas.texto: Paying with your phone goes one step further. When you add a card to Apple Pay, your real card number isn't stored on the phone or on Apple's servers. Your bank creates a separate device account number instead.
Each payment adds a one time security code. So even if a store gets hacked, what leaks can't be used on a website or copied onto a stripe.
Chapter four. The journey.

When you tap, the terminal sends the request to the store's bank, called the acquirer. The acquirer passes it to the card network, Visa or Mastercard. The network routes it to the bank that issued your card.

A lot of that routing happens in a handful of fortress-like data centers. Visa says that at one of them, in Ashburn, Virginia, only seventy five of its employees worldwide are cleared to enter the secure data halls.

visual.pre: Visa's data center in Ashburn, Virginia
visual.label: employees cleared to enter the data halls

escenas.texto: Your bank checks the cryptogram, your available credit, and runs fraud models on the purchase. Visa says it started using AI for fraud detection in nineteen ninety three, and that its AI systems now help prevent more than forty billion dollars of fraud a year.
Then the answer races back the same way. Approved, or declined. The whole round trip usually takes a second or two.
But here's a twist. At that moment, no money has moved. The approval is just a promise, a hold on your credit. The actual money is settled later, usually within a day or two.
Chapter five. Buying online.

visual.sub: when there's no chip to ask

escenas.texto: Online, there's no chip to produce a cryptogram. So the store asks for the three digit code on the back. It proves you probably have the physical card in front of you.

visual.nota: the 3-digit code: proof you're holding the card

escenas.texto: And here's a rule most people don't know. Under the card industry's security standard, called PCI DSS, stores are not allowed to keep that code after the purchase is approved. Not even encrypted. Not even if you ask them to.

For riskier purchases, your bank can step in directly. That's the pop-up asking you to confirm in your banking app, or type a one time code. It's called three D Secure, and it was originally developed by Visa.
Chapter six. Who pays for all this?
You don't pay to swipe. The store does. On every purchase, the store's bank pays a fee to your bank, called interchange.

visual.sub: a fee to your bank on every purchase

escenas.texto: In the United States, credit card interchange has no legal cap, and it averages around two percent. In the European Union, it's capped at zero point three percent for credit cards and zero point two for debit.

That gap is why American cards hand out such generous cash back and travel points. The rewards are paid by the stores, and stores build that cost into their prices. So everyone pays, even people paying cash.
Chapter seven. The real business.

Fees are nice for banks, but the big money is interest. According to the Federal Reserve, the average rate on US credit card accounts paying interest was about twenty two percent a year in August twenty twenty six.

visual.pre: US average APR, accounts paying interest
visual.label: per year (Federal Reserve, Aug 2026)

escenas.texto: And it adds up daily. Most cards divide that yearly rate by three hundred sixty five, and charge it on your balance every single day. Interest starts earning interest.
Let's run the numbers. Say you owe three thousand dollars and only make a typical minimum payment: the interest, plus one percent of the balance.
It takes fifteen years to pay off, and you pay about four thousand five hundred dollars in interest. More than the original debt.
Pay a fixed hundred and fifty a month instead, and you're done in about two years, with under eight hundred dollars of interest.
And if you pay the full statement balance every month, most cards charge no interest at all. Then the card is basically a free short loan, paid for by the store.
Chapter eight. When it goes wrong.

If someone steals your card number in the United States, federal law, the Fair Credit Billing Act from nineteen seventy four, caps what you can owe for unauthorized charges at fifty dollars. Many banks go further and promise zero.

visual.note: report it fast: within 60 days of the statement

escenas.texto: The catch is speed. You have sixty days after the statement arrives to dispute a charge. So the cheapest security tool you have is simply checking your statement every month.

So a credit card is a tiny computer that proves it's real, a trip through four companies in two seconds, a fee hidden in every price, and a loan that can be free, or very expensive. It depends on you.

A fee hidden in every price
